title: Programmatic Ops and Safe Tooling Demo - Peloton Analytics
summary: Redwood AE + SE ran through JSON mode, schema-driven tool calls, and runtime guardrails with Peloton Analytics. Demonstrated Console flows for rule-based fallbacks, Canary rollouts, and Optimize suggestions (batching/quantization). Security questions (SOC2, KMS, SSO) surfaced; next steps agreed: pilot data set + benchmark run, security packet + pricing, and a follow-up technical deep-dive to scope private deployment.
next_steps: Redwood: send security packet (SOC2, ISO, KMS detail) by 2027-09-17
Peloton: share sample prompt set and 1 week of anonymized inference traces by 2027-09-21
Schedule technical deep dive (private deployment options) for week of 2027-09-27
Run a 24 hour benchmark on Redwood Dedicated trial - Redwood to provision test capacity
action_items: Jordan - Share security slides + SOC2 report by 2027-09-17
Priya - Upload demo walkthrough recording and console bookmarks (JSON examples)
Marcus - Provide sample prompts and target latency SLOs by 2027-09-21
Devin - Confirm encryption/KMS vendor requirements and any HSM needs
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (SE), Liam (SE), Marcus (Peloton Head of ML), Sara (Eng Manager), Devin (SecOps), Amrita (Data Platform)

Auto-summary: Walkthrough of Redwood's JSON mode and guarded tool-calling workflow. Live demo in Console showing schema enforcement, typed responses, runtime policy-based fallbacks, and Optimize suggestions for batch/quantization to reduce cost while holding latency targets. Security and deployment questions discussed; pilot and follow-up steps agreed.

--- Transcript body (timestamps approx):
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining uh appreciate you carving out time today, this is Jordan from Redwood. We've got Priya and Liam from the SE team with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Marcus: good thanks, excited to see the flow. we've been talking internally about moving more of our inference from the open-source infra to a managed inference lane so curious about the safety and typed outputs.
[00:18] Priya: great. quick agenda - we'll show JSON mode via the API and Console, then run a tool-calling example where the model emits a typed action that triggers an internal enrichment call. after that we'll show the Optimize suggestions and discuss deployment modes and security. we can deep-dive as needed. sound ok?
[00:31] Sara: yup perfect. Devin will ask the security q's later.
[00:36] Liam: quick note: we'll also simulate a fallback from a higher-capacity model to a lower-cost variant if latency spikes.
[00:44] Marcus: important for us, yeah. we need predictable tail latencies under 250 ms for short prompts.
[00:51] Priya: ok great, we'll show latency vs cost knobs.

[02:05] Priya: starting the Console — you'll see a sample app we preloaded. first, JSON mode: we give the model a strict output schema for a 'customer_profile_update' action. Schema enforces types and required fields — name, account_id, update_type, confidence_score, and optional metadata. watch how the runtime validates and rejects malformed shapes.
[02:28] (screen share: Console, JSON schema pasted)
[02:34] Priya: here's the prompt + schema, I'm going to hit run. note the runtime options: enforce_schema: true, max_tokens: 256, model: rwd-5b-quant (we selected a quantized variant for cost demo).
[02:47] Speaker 1: (mutter) ok we are at 62% CPU on this host.
[03:02] Priya: result returns — model produced a JSON payload that matched schema. Console shows a typed diff highlighting missing fields were auto-filled, and we have a 'validation_score' for the schema conformance. sometimes the transcription engine shows 'valid a shun' — sorry, validation score.
[03:19] Marcus: i like the diff view. does the runtime ever coerce types? for example, if account_id comes back as number vs string?
[03:28] Priya: good q. by default it will flag a schema violation as an error. you can flip a permissive mode that will coerce string<->number for backwards compat, but we recommend strict enforcement for production actions. coercion is logged in audit trails.
[03:42] Devin: how are those audit trails stored? we need immutable logs for compliance.
[03:48] Liam: logs are exported to your S3 or GCS bucket with object versioning, and we also forward audit events to your SIEM via webhook. we support customer-managed KMS for envelope encryption. for highest assurance we support HSM-backed KMS.
[04:05] Devin: ok can we get the KMS spec and the key rotation cadence?
[04:09] Jordan: yes we'll attach our KMS doc in the security packet — action item.

[05:12] Priya: next demo: function/tool calling. we have a tiny enrichment lambda that fetches canonical company metadata from Peloton's internal service. the model is constrained to emit an action object called 'enrich_company' with fields: domain, enrich_level. Redwood's runtime will validate the output against the schema and, on success, call the configured webhook.
[05:32] (console: run demo)
[05:37] Priya: model emits action, runtime invokes webhook, we show the outbound call trace and the KV cache entry. note the call trace includes a signature header we inject so Peloton can verify the request.
[05:47] Marcus: nice. is there a retry policy? what about idempotency?
[05:53] Priya: yes — retry policy configurable per-route with exponential backoff and idempotency keys derived from the action payload. you can set max_attempts and a dead-letter queue.
[06:02] Sara: for our use case we need strong at-most-once semantics for billing events; can the runtime disable retries?
[06:09] Liam: absolutely, you can set retries=0 and route failures to DLQ; we also support synchronous+async modes so you can choose immediate failures vs queued processing.

[07:30] Marcus: walk me through guardrails — suppose the model produces an action that would delete records, how do we prevent unsafe ops?
[07:38] Priya: good scenario. we have policy rules at two levels: schema-level and runtime policy. schema-level just checks shape. runtime policies are more expressive — you can deny based on fields (e.g., delete=true) or require human approval when confidence_score < threshold. we also have canary rollouts that route a fraction of calls to a human-in-the-loop pathway.
[07:58] Devin: can those policies be enforced in Dedicated or Private deployments? we need them inside our VPC.
[08:05] Jordan: yes, policies are enforced in all modes. for Private (VPC) the control plane can be self-hosted with the policy engine running inside your tenancy.

[09:10] Priya: switching to Optimize — this is our suggestions engine. It looks at token distribution and sequence lengths in your trace and recommends batching, KV-cache prefixes and quantization profiles. for your short SLM-style prompts, Optimize suggests small batch sizes (4-8) to keep p99 latency under your 250ms target while using rwd-8b-llm-qs quant profile for cost reduction.
[09:37] Marcus: what's the expected cost delta if we do that?
[09:41] Priya: rough ballpark — quantized model + batching reduces per-token cost by 35-50% depending on hit-rate and cache effectiveness. we'll send a modeled estimate for your workload once you share traces.
[09:53] Marcus: ok, please do.

[11:02] Jordan: a quick note on fallbacks: you can define a routing policy - primary model with strict schema enforcement, fallback model (cheaper or smaller) with permissive mode and additional post-parse validation. if fallback yields a different shape, the runtime can automatically enrich, call retry policies, or escalate. we demoed this earlier on a simulated load spike.
[11:29] Sara: is the fallback automatic or can we gate it behind canary percent? we want control.
[11:35] Liam: fully configurable. you set thresholds: queue_wait_ms, model_saturation, or error_rate to trigger fallback. also manual promos via the Console.

[13:10] Priya: demo of canary - create rollout 10% to new model variant; Console shows per-route metrics and a diff of typed outputs to compare quality regressions. you can set automatic rollback on quality regression above your threshold.
[13:30] Marcus: are those quality checks based on prompt sets? we need stable evals over a set of golden prompts.
[13:36] Priya: yes — Redwood hooks into your eval suite. you can pin a prompt set and we calculate regression metrics per rollout. if the new variant fails the regression test, rollback triggers.

[15:00] Devin: security again — SOC2, ISO, SSO. we require SAML SSO and fine-grained RBAC for console access. we also need audit logs retained for two years.
[15:12] Jordan: we support SAML, OIDC, and SCIM provisioning. RBAC is role-based with route-level permissions. Audit retention can be configured; for long-term retention we ship to customer-managed storage. SOC2 report and ISO certs will be shared.
[15:25] Amrita: do you support data residency EU-only?
[15:28] Liam: region pinning is available; we can host inference nodes in EU regions and keep logs in EU storage.

[17:45] Priya: back to JSON mode — one caveat: model hallucination still happens. schema enforcement helps catch shape errors but not semantic hallucination. our recommended pattern is layered checks: schema -> static validators -> dynamic business rules -> human approval for high-risk ops.
[18:03] Marcus: makes sense. can we run a pilot that includes the full chain?
[18:09] Jordan: yep, pilot scope we suggested: 2-week trial on Dedicated capacity, run your sample prompts at production QPS, measure p50/p95/p99, and validate typed-action success rate.

[20:20] Sara: regarding billing and cost predictability, how do reserved capacity commits vs pay-as-you-go compare?
[20:27] Jordan: dedicated reserved capacity gives predictable throughput for a flat monthly fee with overage options. pay-as-you-go (hosted API) is per-token. for heavy sustained workloads Dedicated is typically 30-60% cheaper on unit economics depending on commit level. Optimize helps further reduce unit cost.

[22:10] Priya: questions about logs: we annotate every request with route_id, model_variant, schema_hash, and validation flags, so you can query which requests passed or failed schema checks.
[22:22] Devin: that annotation is great. can we mask PII in logs?
[22:26] Liam: yes — redact rules at ingestion can scrub or hash fields; we also support token-sampling and differential retention.

[25:00] (demo: console - route creation and policy editor)
[25:09] Priya: here's the policy DSL — it's yaml-ish and you can quickly add rule: deny if action.type == 'delete' and confidence_score < 0.95. you can also inject a webhook approval step.
[25:28] Marcus: can the DSL be templatized and stored as git?
[25:33] Priya: yes, policies can be exported and stored in your Git repo; we also have a policy-as-code workflow with patch reviews.

[28:45] Sara: operationally, what's the observability footprint — do you provide token-level tracing?
[28:51] Priya: we provide token-level cost & latency breakdowns at sample granularity, plus full trace logs for errors. in Dedicated/Private you can increase retention.

[31:12] Marcus: latency again — for short prompts can you get under 200ms p95?
[31:18] Liam: with appropriate batching and pinned model variants yes, many customers see p95 ~120-180ms for short prompts on Dedicated. p99 will be higher; Optimize helps push down p99 by suggesting batching and cache prefixes.

[33:00] Priya: demo: now we'll show a toolchain where model output triggers an enrichment, the enrichment writes to a staging DB and we run a small webhook that returns structured enrichment; runtime merges that back into the action payload and completes the typed response. watch the trace for the merge and the idempotency key.
[33:22] (demo runs)
[33:31] Marcus: love the merge trace. question: does the enrich call leak raw prompt text to the webhook? we can't expose PII.
[33:39] Priya: by default we don't forward source_prompt unless you opt in; you can configure redaction rules per route.

[36:00] Devin: compliance - do you keep a tamper-evident log?
[36:05] Jordan: we provide signed audit logs and can enable append-only storage with object locking on your bucket for immutability.

[38:45] Sara: what about developer ergonomics — how do our engineers test their prompt/schema changes?
[38:52] Priya: Console has a 'playground' route where developers can run samples against a staging model, capture outputs, and run unit tests against schemas. we also provide a CLI for local validation against our schema library so you can run CI checks.

[41:10] Marcus: ok so next steps — we want the security packet and the pilot details. can you also run a short benchmark against a 24hr window with our traces?
[41:21] Jordan: yes. we'll provision a Dedicated trial instance and run a 24hr benchmark; we'll need your traces and a contact for access.

[43:00] Priya: one more note: fallback orchestration can include a 'safety shim' — a lightweight model that verifies outputs against business rules before executing high-risk actions. it's cheap and reduces false positives in the main pipeline.
[43:16] Marcus: ok put that into the pilot scope.

[45:30] (brief pause, folks taking notes)
[45:40] Devin: if we go Private, what's the upgrade path? we may start Hosted, then Dedicated, then Private months later.
[45:47] Jordan: many customers follow that path. Redwood's config is portable — route definitions, schemas, and policy DSL move between modes. there are network and key management steps for Private, we'll detail those in the deep-dive.

[48:10] Sara: anything else on price negotiation?
[48:14] Jordan: pricing will reflect pilot size and commit level. we'll include pilot credits and a recommended commit bracket in our proposal.

[50:00] Priya: recap — demo showed JSON-mode schema enforcement, typed tool calling, runtime guardrails, fallbacks, Optimize recommendations. action items: security packet, shared traces, and schedule technical deep-dive.
[50:18] Marcus: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[50:22] Jordan: thanks all, we'll follow up with notes and the packet.
[50:27] (meeting closes)

Post-meeting notes: Redwood to attach security artifacts (SOC2, ISO certs, KMS/HSM spec), a proposed pilot plan and cost model, and console bookmarks with the schema examples used in the demo. Peloton to share anonymized traces and acceptance criteria (latency, success-rate).
